background.definition: Accidental hypothermia is an unintentional reduction in the body's core temperature to less than 95.0°F or 35°C. This differs from intentional hypothermia that is induced in certain medical situations, which will not be covered here.

list.listitem: Each year 700 deaths due to hypothermia in the United States.
In North America and Europe, about 150 people are killed each year in avalanches.
Accidental hypothermia occurs when the ability of the body to generate heat is superseded by heat loss. This may occur even in the summer when a cool mountain wind blows on summer hikers.

While this typically occurs in cold environments where the ambient temperature is well below normal body temperature, it can also occur at normal room temperatures if the body's thermoregulatory systems are disrupted by disease or injury.
Wind and wetness can precipitate hypothermia even in only moderately cold temperatures, and water immersion can create hypothermia even in warm tropical waters.

Humans maintain a uniform body temperature by internal generation of heat. Stability of body temperature results from a balance between internal heat production and heat loss to the environment. When core temperature falls, adaptive behaviors such as putting on a coat or moving to a warmer environment decrease heat loss. Additionally, voluntary or involuntary muscle activity in the form of movement or shivering increases heat production.
Disease states that affect cognition or motor function predispose patients to hypothermia when these behaviors or autoregulation fail to occur, such as malnutrition and dementia.

Heat is lost or gained through radiation (55%), evaporation (30%), conduction (15%), and convection (minor). Wet clothing or immersion in water causes more rapid heat loss because water is 25 times more conductive than air. Since core temperature is usually above ambient temperature, heat transfer is usually out of the body.

Primary hypothermia results from failure of heat generation in a cold environment. This can occur even when the difference between ambient and core temperature is small. Medical conditions such as strokes or other injuries may prevent muscle activity or behavioral responses to cold, causing or worsening hypothermia.

Secondary hypothermia results when a disease state interferes with thermoregulation. Onset of hypothermia can be triggered by events similar to the generation of primary hypothermia, and primary and secondary hypothermia may exist concurrently.
People who participate in outdoor recreation should become familiar with weather patterns, qualities of outdoor clothing, and take sensible precautions prior to undertaking the activity. C
Elderly patients with chronic medical conditions should have adequate clothing and coverings. C

The potential for heat loss and the risk of hypothermia should be considered in all patients with a serious medical condition, especially in those in whom there is anticipated difficulty with behavioral adaptations to cold. C
The diagnosis of hypothermia should be considered in all patients with trauma, cardiac arrest, and other unexplainable symptoms. C
Temperature should be taken with a rectal thermometer that is capable of reading low temperatures. C

list.listitem: The diagnosis of hypothermia is made when the core temperature is below 35°C (95°F). There are no strict criteria for the diagnosis of hypothermia beyond that the core temperature is usually below 35°C (95°F). It may be classified as mild (32°C-35°C), moderate (28°C-32°C), and severe (<28°C).
Hypothermia should not be diagnosed when the core temperature is normal.
Standard thermometers do not read below 34.4°C. Use a rectal thermometer capable of reading low body temperatures.
Hypothermia is present when the core temperature is less than 95°F.

Hypothermia may result from direct exposure to cold or be due to heat loss while incapacitated from another illness. A high index of suspicion is essential, especially when caring for elderly patients or in patients presenting with unexplained symptoms since symptoms of a primary condition may overshadow the symptoms of hypothermia.

Signs and symptoms can be roughly correlated to core temperature and are listed below:
Mild hypothermia (32°C-35°C or 89.6°F-95°F): tachypnea, impaired judgment, lethargy, confusion, vasoconstriction, apathy, tachycardia, hypertension, ataxia, dysarthria, loss of fine motor coordination, and shivering. Moderate hypothermia (28°C-32°C or 82.4°F-89.6°F): shivering stops, decreased level of consciousness, bradycardia, dilated pupils, slowed reflexes, delirium, J-wave on electrocardiogram (ECG), and diuresis. Severe hypothermia (<28°C or 82.4°F): unresponsiveness or coma, may appear dead, hypotension, apnea, areflexia, pulmonary edema, acidosis, ventricular fibrillation, or asystole. Vague symptoms of mild hypothermia may include hunger, nausea, confusion, dizziness, chills, pruritus, or dyspnea.
There are no tests that are specific or diagnostic for hypothermia except the measurement of core temperature with an accurate rectal thermometer.
Results of laboratory testing may be helpful in determining whether hypothermia was the result of or the cause of the clinical condition.

Patients with hypothermia present with a variety of metabolic abnormalities. Obtain a complete blood count (CBC), electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, and glucose. Arterial blood gases are useful to assess for acidosis. A coagulation profile can be used to diagnose coagulopathies. An ECG is necessary to evaluate for arrhythmias, although no arrhythmia is typical for hypothermia.

Additional laboratory testing or imaging may be ordered depending on the clinical scenario. For example, A computed tomographic (CT) scan of the head will be helpful in evaluating a trauma victim or if a CVA is expected.
Treatment should begin in the prehospital setting: remove from the cold, remove wet clothing, passively rewarm victim, and stabilize associated injuries.
Obtain a CBC, electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose, arterial blood gases, coagulation profile, and ECG. Consider head CT if stroke or trauma is suspected.
See for a summary of treatment options.
Perform cardiopulmonary resuscitation if appropriate. Follow routine ACLS and ATLS guidelines when appropriate, and Wilderness Society Guidelines for pre-hospital management.C
Treat only life-threatening arrhythmias. Defibrillate at 2 J/kg (or the biphasic equivalent) if the patient is in ventricular fibrillation or ventricular tachycardia. C
Use amiodarone for treatment of ventricular fibrillation. Withhold intravenous (IV) drugs if core temperature is less than 30°C. C

Start a large bore IV line. Volume administration is recommended with an initial bolus of 250 to 500 cc of 5% dextrose in isotonic sodium chloride solution. Hypotension is treated by volume replacement and rewarming. C
Chose a method of rewarming—active or passive based on degree of hypothermia and available resources. C
Medications do not play a major role in treatment of hypothermia except in specific situations such as arrhythmias when rewarming.
Routine use of steroids, barbiturates, and antibiotics have not been shown to increase survival rates.
Since many medications have little effect if core temperature is less than 30°C, these are often withheld until core temperature is above this value.
Amiodarone is recommended for treatment of ventricular fibrillation.

Treatment usually begins in the prehospital environment. Remove from the cold environment, remove wet clothing, and passively rewarm the victim. Associated injuries must be stabilized. Avoid rough handling of the patient as it may precipitate ventricular arrhythmias.

The International Commission for Mountain Emergency Medicine (ICAR MedCom) recommends the following classification system for hypothermic patients based on AVPU (alert, verbal, pain, unresponsive) scale and vitals: Stage 1 (low risk of cardiac arrest) = Alert from AVPU; Stage 2 (moderate risk of cardiac arrest) = Verbal from AVPU; Stage 3 (high risk of cardiac arrest) = Painful or Unconscious from AVPU and vital signs present, and Stage 4 (hypothermic cardiac arrest) = Unconscious and no detectable vital signs.

Wilderness Medical Society Guidelines (2014) recommend out-of-hospital treatment based on the severity of hypotermia as follows:
Mild hypothermia (32°C-35°C or 89.6°F-95°F): Patient has normal metal status, but is not able to function and care for self, and is shivering, with temp 32°C to 35°C. Protect from further cooling, seek shelter, remove wet clothing once in shelter, support shivering with warmed, high calorie food or drink, no standing or walking for 30 minutes, and consider active warming (see moderate hypothermia). Evacuate if no improvement in 30 minutes. Moderate hypothermia (28°C-32°C or 82.4°F-89.6°F): Patient does not have normal mental status, is hivering, and is conscious, temp 28°C to 32°C. Treat as for mild hypotheramia, provide active warming with heat to upper torso, chest, axillae, and back using large heating pads, forced air, or Norwegian Heat Pac. Provide peripheral IV or interosseous or femoral line. Provide volume replacement with warm 40°C to 42°C saline boluses. Keep horizontal, no standing or walking. Severe/profound hypothermia (<28°C or 82.4°F): Patient is unconscious, but with signs of life and normal rhythm on ECG and patient has respiration and pulse (check for up to 1 minute). Treat as for moderate hypothermia above, plus CPR and intubation if no signs of life. No CPR if signs of life present or perfusing rhythm seen; consider transcutaneous pacing if bracycardia with hypotension. Evacuate the patient carefully Death: If the patient has an obviously lethal injury, the chest is too stiff for CPR, the patient was buried in avalanche for more than 35 minutes, or airway is obstructed by snow, recommendation is to not attempt resuscitation.

If indicated, basic life support and advanced life support protocols are followed. Defibrillation by an automated external defibrillator is recommended for prehospital use in hypothermia. No data exist to guide at which temperature defibrillation attempts should be made, but success rates are low if the core temperature is less than 32°C. If the core temperature is less than 30°C, give a maximum of 3 shocks for ventricular fibrillation/ventricular tachycardia until core temperature is increased, and give IV medications at longer than standard intervals.

Because many arrhythmias convert spontaneously upon rewarming, aggressive therapy of minor arrhythmias is not warranted. Transient ventricular arrhythmias, bradycardia, or any atrial arrhythmias should not be treated.

Indications for intubation are the same as in a normothermic patient. Coagulopathies are common in patients with hypothermia; methods of intubation that pose the least risk of trauma are recommended. Avoid overzealous ventilation because hypocapnia can increase ventricular irritability.
Nasogastric tube placement may be warranted to relieve gastric distention.

Hypothermic patients will have vasodilatation on rewarming, and fluid administration is recommended with an initial bolus of 250 to 500 cc of 5% dextrose in isotonic sodium chloride solution. IV fluids should be heated to 40°C to 42°C if possible. Rapid fluid resuscitation may be necessary. Use of vasopressors for hypotension and ventricular fibrillation is controversial, although human studies have shown little benefit.

Definitive treatment is rewarming the patient. Controversy exists regarding the best method to rewarm patients. As a result, the best method depends on the degree of temperature depression, local expertise, and availability (). Remember, no one is dead until they are warm and dead.

For avalanche victims, recent evidence-based guidelines have been published. If lethal injuries are excluded and the body is not frozen and the burial time is <35 minutes OR the core temperature is >32°C, rapid extrication and standard ALS is important. If burial time is >35 minutes and the core temperature is <32°C, gentle extrication, full body insulation, ECG and core-temperature monitoring and airway management is recommended. Cardiopulmonary bypass rewarming or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation is recommended for patients with cardiac instability or in cardiac arrest (with a patent airway).

A systematic review identified 19 case reports or case series of 47 adults receiving extracorporeal life support (ECLS) following accidential hypothermia with hemodynamic instability. Median body temperature was 24.6 C, and median Glasgow Coma Scale on presentation was 3 (IQR 3 to 7), with cardiac arrest occuring in 75%. Median time to ECLS was 2.5 hours, and median duration of ECLS was 18 hours (IQR 4 to 27 hours). The median length of hospital stay was 17 days, with 9 of 47 patients dying in the hospital and another 6 having minor long-term cognitive impairment.
The goal of treatment is to return body temperature to a normal 97.8°F or 37°C.

Most patients with severe hypothermia will be admitted to the intensive care unit. Consultation with a critical care specialist is recommended for severely hypothermic patients or if the clinician has limited clinical experience.

Mild hypothermia might be self-correcting if heat loss is minimized and the cause of hypothermia is identified and treated. Otherwise, hypothermia is a medical emergency that requires definitive treatment. C
The outcomes of severe hypothermia are variable, and generally worse in patients with major comorbidities, greater degree of hypothermia, and greater length of time with hypothermia. B
An admission temperatures less than 35°C is associated with much higher mortality than temperature of 35°C or more (25.5% vs 3.0%, P < .001). B

A systematic review found that (1) serum potassium less than 7 mmol/L and (2) patent airway in patients buried for more than 35 minutes or when temperature is less than 32°C are associated with improved prognosis. B

tr.td: Passive external warming
Slow, generating only 0.5°C-2°C/h. The patient is insulated from further heat loss and warms themselves
This method is useful for mild cases with no underlying disease
Active external warming
Useful in mild cases

External heat is applied in a noninvasive manner. Pooled blood in the extremities may result in a return of incompletely rewarmed blood to the central circulation. Rewarming the trunk alone may minimize this problem
Humidified oxygen, heated infusions and heated inhalation
Safe and effective as adjunctive therapy
Should be used in all patients during rewarming

Can rewarm as fast as 2.4°C/h
Immersion in water bath at 40°C
Monitoring and resuscitation are difficult
Active core rewarming
Gastric and colonic lavage
Limited by surface area and should be used as an adjunct to other methods
Regurgitation is common
Mediastinal lavage and closed thoracic lavage
Invasive. The organs are bathed with isotonic sodium chloride solution heated to 40°C
Should be used only if cardiopulmonary bypass is immediately available or the patient is in full cardiac arrest
Peritoneal lavage
Available at most hospitals. A standard 1.5% dextrose dialysate is heated to 40°C-45°C. Rewarming averages 1°C-3°C/h
This method may help detoxification in drug overdose and rewarms the liver faster than other methods. Not routinely advocated for stable patients
Extracorporeal blood rewarming. Hemodialysis. Cardiopulmonary bypass. Atriovenous rewarming. Venovenous rewarming
Fast, rising core temperature 1°C-2°C every 3-5 min
Requires considerable skill to perform and may require systemic anticoagulation. Can be used by specialists experienced in these techniques for severe hypothermia
